subject: Neurology
vignette: A 45-year-old woman with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease undergoes screening and is found to have a saccular aneurysm at a bifurcation of the circle of Willis. She has been entirely asymptomatic.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this aneurysm?

options.text: A microaneurysm of a lenticulostriate artery caused by chronic hypertension
A berry aneurysm at a circle-of-Willis bifurcation, often silent until rupture
A fusiform basilar aneurysm caused by atherosclerosis
A Charcot-Bouchard aneurysm that is not visible on angiography
An arteriovenous malformation

explanation_correct: Saccular (berry) aneurysms are abnormal dilations that occur at bifurcations in the circle of Willis, with the most common site being the junction of the anterior communicating and anterior cerebral arteries. They are associated with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and risk increases with advanced age, hypertension, and tobacco smoking. They are usually clinically silent until rupture, the most common complication, which causes subarachnoid hemorrhage. Unruptured aneurysms can also compress adjacent structures.

explanation_incorrect.A: Lenticulostriate Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms are hypertensive small-vessel lesions causing intraparenchymal hemorrhage, not saccular aneurysms at circle-of-Willis bifurcations.
explanation_incorrect.C: A fusiform basilar aneurysm from atherosclerosis is not the berry aneurysm described; berry aneurysms are saccular, occur at bifurcations, and are linked to polycystic kidney disease.
explanation_incorrect.D: Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms are not visible on angiography and are associated with chronic hypertension rather than polycystic kidney disease; the lesion here is saccular.
explanation_incorrect.E: An arteriovenous malformation is a congenital tangle of vessels that can hemorrhage, but it is not a saccular dilation at a circle-of-Willis bifurcation associated with polycystic kidney disease.

educationalObjective: Berry aneurysms occur at circle-of-Willis bifurcations, are associated with ADPKD and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and are usually silent until rupture causes subarachnoid hemorrhage.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 50-year-old man has a large aneurysm at the anterior communicating artery that compresses the optic chiasm and then ruptures.
question: Which of the following combinations of findings is most consistent with this aneurysm?

options.text: Bitemporal hemianopia from compression; contralateral lower-extremity weakness from anterior cerebral artery ischemia after rupture
Homonymous hemianopia from optic tract compression; contralateral upper-extremity weakness after middle cerebral artery ischemia
Ipsilateral blown pupil and down-and-out eye from CN III compression
Fluent word-salad speech from temporal lobe compression
Nonfluent speech with intact comprehension from frontal lobe compression

explanation_correct: An anterior communicating artery aneurysm can compress the optic chiasm, producing bitemporal hemianopia and visual acuity deficits. If it ruptures, it causes ischemia in the anterior cerebral artery distribution, leading to contralateral lower-extremity hemiparesis and sensory deficits. The anterior communicating artery-anterior cerebral artery junction is the most common site of saccular aneurysms.

explanation_incorrect.B: Optic tract or middle cerebral artery involvement would produce homonymous hemianopia and contralateral upper-extremity and lower-face deficits, which are not the classic anterior communicating artery compression and rupture pattern.
explanation_incorrect.C: An ipsilateral blown pupil with a down-and-out eye is the classic finding of a posterior communicating artery aneurysm compressing CN III, not an anterior communicating artery aneurysm.
explanation_incorrect.D: Word-salad fluent aphasia implies Wernicke area involvement, not the chiasmal compression and anterior cerebral artery ischemia of an anterior communicating artery aneurysm.
explanation_incorrect.E: Nonfluent speech with intact comprehension implies Broca area involvement; an anterior communicating artery aneurysm instead causes bitemporal hemianopia and lower-extremity deficits.

educationalObjective: Anterior communicating artery aneurysms compress the optic chiasm causing bitemporal hemianopia and, if ruptured, cause anterior cerebral artery lower-extremity deficits.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 58-year-old woman presents with a sudden severe headache and is found to have a dilated right pupil. On examination her right eye is deviated downward and outward, with ptosis.
question: Which aneurysm location best explains these findings?

options.text: Anterior communicating artery aneurysm
Middle cerebral artery aneurysm
Posterior communicating artery aneurysm
Basilar tip aneurysm
Anterior cerebral artery aneurysm

explanation_correct: A posterior communicating artery aneurysm can compress the adjacent oculomotor nerve (CN III), producing an ipsilateral CN III palsy with mydriasis (a blown pupil), ptosis, and a down-and-out eye from unopposed CN IV and CN VI activity. Posterior communicating artery aneurysms are a classic cause of painful isolated CN III palsy. Rupture would also produce subarachnoid hemorrhage.

explanation_incorrect.A: An anterior communicating artery aneurysm compresses the optic chiasm, causing bitemporal hemianopia, and if ruptured causes anterior cerebral artery lower-extremity deficits, not an isolated CN III palsy.
explanation_incorrect.B: A middle cerebral artery aneurysm, if ruptured, causes ischemia with contralateral upper-extremity and lower-face hemiparesis, not an isolated blown pupil.
explanation_incorrect.D: A basilar tip aneurysm can compress nearby structures but is not the classic cause of an isolated ipsilateral blown pupil and down-and-out eye.
explanation_incorrect.E: An anterior cerebral artery aneurysm rupture would cause contralateral lower-extremity deficits, not the CN III findings described here.

educationalObjective: Posterior communicating artery aneurysms compress CN III to produce an ipsilateral blown pupil, ptosis, and a down-and-out eye.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 70-year-old man with chronic hypertension presents with sudden right-arm and right-lower-face weakness and sensory loss. Imaging shows ischemia in the left middle cerebral artery territory and also notes small-vessel changes deep in the brain that are not visualized on angiography.
question: Which of the following statements about these findings is correct?

options.text: The small deep lesions are berry aneurysms at circle-of-Willis bifurcations
The deficits are most consistent with anterior cerebral artery territory ischemia
The small vessels are Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms that are clearly visible on angiography
The ischemia fits a middle cerebral artery aneurysm rupture, and the deep lesions are Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms
These findings indicate amyloid angiopathy as the underlying cause

explanation_correct: Rupture of a middle cerebral artery aneurysm causes ischemia in the middle cerebral artery distribution, producing contralateral upper-extremity and lower-facial hemiparesis with sensory deficits. Separately, chronic hypertension produces Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms in small penetrating vessels such as lenticulostriate arteries in the basal ganglia and thalamus, which can cause intraparenchymal hemorrhagic strokes and are characteristically not visible on angiography. This distinguishes them from berry aneurysms.

explanation_incorrect.A: Berry aneurysms are saccular dilations at circle-of-Willis bifurcations that rupture into the subarachnoid space, not small deep parenchymal vessel lesions.
explanation_incorrect.B: Anterior cerebral artery territory ischemia would predominantly affect the contralateral lower extremity, not the upper extremity and lower face seen in middle cerebral artery ischemia.
explanation_incorrect.C: Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms are specifically described as not visible on angiography, so stating they are clearly visible is incorrect.
explanation_incorrect.E: Amyloid angiopathy causes lobar hemorrhages in older adults and is not related to hypertension-induced microaneurysms or this middle cerebral artery ischemic pattern.

educationalObjective: Middle cerebral artery aneurysm rupture causes upper-extremity and lower-face deficits, while Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms are hypertensive small-vessel lesions invisible on angiography.
